title: Systems Programming
blurb: Python systems programming: files, processes, threads, IPC, sockets, synchronization, and operating-system resource management.
description: Learn systems-level concepts through Python APIs and safe browser simulations.

lessons.title: Memory, lifetime & resource ownership
lessons.explanation: Systems programming makes resource lifetime explicit. Stack storage typically follows scope and call lifetime, while heap objects can outlive the function that created them.
commonMistakes: Acquiring files, locks, sockets, or other resources without a guaranteed cleanup path.
lessons.explain: Systems programming makes resource lifetime explicit. Stack storage typically follows scope and call lifetime, while heap objects can outlive the function that created them.

lessons.title: References, mutability & ownership
objectives: Choose shallow or deep copying intentionally
lessons.explanation: A reference identifies an existing object rather than copying its full contents. With mutable objects, two names can refer to the same object, so a change through one reference can be observed through the other.
examples:
import copy
original = {"items": [1, 2]}
clone = copy.deepcopy(original)
clone["items"].append(3)
print(original, clone)
commonMistakes: Confusing assignment, shallow copy, and deep copy.
lessons.explain: A reference identifies an existing object rather than copying its full contents. With mutable objects, two names can refer to the same object, so a change through one reference can be observed through the other.

lessons.title: Files, descriptors & OS boundaries
lessons.explanation: Operating systems expose files and many devices through descriptor-like handles. A program asks the kernel to read, write, open, close, or otherwise operate on those resources through system-call boundaries.
examples:
import os, tempfile
fd, path = tempfile.mkstemp()
os.write(fd, b"hello")
os.lseek(fd, 0, 0)
print(os.read(fd, 5).decode())
os.close(fd)
os.unlink(path)
commonMistakes: Assuming every read/write completes exactly as requested or ignoring OS errors.
lessons.explain: Operating systems expose files and many devices through descriptor-like handles. A program asks the kernel to read, write, open, close, or otherwise operate on those resources through system-call boundaries.

lessons.title: Processes & program execution
lessons.explanation: A process is an executing program with its own address space, resources, environment, and operating-system identity. Starting a subprocess creates a separate execution context; the parent can pass arguments/environment, capture output, and inspect the exit status.
examples:
import subprocess
result = subprocess.run(["python", "-c", "print(6 * 7)"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(result.returncode, result.stdout.strip())
commonMistakes: Launching commands without checking the exit status or safely separating command arguments.
lessons.explain: A process is an executing program with its own address space, resources, environment, and operating-system identity. Starting a subprocess creates a separate execution context; the parent can pass arguments/environment, capture output, and inspect the exit status.

lessons.title: Threads, races & synchronization
lessons.explanation: Threads share process memory, which makes communication cheap but also allows data races when multiple threads access shared mutable state without safe coordination. Locks protect critical sections, condition variables let threads wait for state changes, and queues often provide a clearer ownership boundary for work.
examples:
from threading import Lock
lock = Lock()
total = 0
with lock:
    total += 1
print(total)
commonMistakes: Sharing mutable state between threads without a synchronization plan.
lessons.explain: Threads share process memory, which makes communication cheap but also allows data races when multiple threads access shared mutable state without safe coordination. Locks protect critical sections, condition variables let threads wait for state changes, and queues often provide a clearer ownership boundary for work.

lessons.title: IPC: pipes, sockets & shared memory
lessons.explanation: Inter-process communication moves information across process boundaries. Pipes provide a byte stream commonly used between related processes, sockets support local or networked communication, and shared memory can avoid copying but requires careful synchronization and a defined memory layout.
examples:
from multiprocessing import Pipe
left, right = Pipe()
left.send({"type": "job", "id": 7})
print(right.recv())
commonMistakes: Sending bytes through a pipe or socket without a framing/protocol rule.
lessons.explain: Inter-process communication moves information across process boundaries. Pipes provide a byte stream commonly used between related processes, sockets support local or networked communication, and shared memory can avoid copying but requires careful synchronization and a defined memory layout.

lessons.title: Concurrency design & worker pools
lessons.explanation: Worker pools bound concurrency by keeping a controlled number of workers that take tasks from a queue. This is different from starting an unlimited thread or process for every request.
examples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def work(value):
    return value * value

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
    print(list(pool.map(work, [2, 3, 4, 5])))
lessons.explain: Worker pools bound concurrency by keeping a controlled number of workers that take tasks from a queue. This is different from starting an unlimited thread or process for every request.

lessons.title: Profiling & systems debugging
lessons.explanation: Profiling and debugging answer different questions. A debugger helps inspect control flow and state around a correctness failure, while a profiler measures where time or memory is actually spent.
examples:
import time
start = time.perf_counter()
result = sum(i * i for i in range(10000))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(result, round(elapsed, 6))
lessons.explain: Profiling and debugging answer different questions. A debugger helps inspect control flow and state around a correctness failure, while a profiler measures where time or memory is actually spent.

exercises.title: Guaranteed resource cleanup
exercises.prompt: Open a simulated resource through a context manager, deliberately raise an exception while using it, and prove that cleanup still happens. Explain why relying on a later garbage-collection cycle is not enough for OS resources.

exercises.title: Reference vs copy bug
exercises.prompt: Create nested mutable data, make both a shared reference and a copy, then change the nested value. Explain which objects changed and choose a copying strategy when independent state is required.

exercises.title: Safe low-level file I/O
exercises.prompt: Model reading and writing through a file descriptor or file object with explicit error handling and guaranteed close/cleanup. Demonstrate the normal path and a missing/unreadable file path.

exercises.title: Subprocess result handling
exercises.prompt: Run a harmless child process, capture stdout/stderr, inspect its exit status, and treat a non-zero status as a failure instead of assuming that process creation means success.

exercises.title: Process environment boundary
exercises.prompt: Launch a child process with a controlled environment value and show that changing the child environment does not mutate the parent process environment. Explain the isolation boundary.

exercises.title: Reproduce a race condition
exercises.prompt: Use multiple workers to update shared state in a deliberately unsafe way or simulated interleaving. Show the incorrect result and explain why the failure depends on timing.

exercises.title: Protect a critical section
exercises.prompt: Fix a shared-state update by protecting the smallest necessary critical section with synchronization. Compare the result with the unsafe version and explain the cost of excessive locking.

exercises.title: Producer-consumer queue
exercises.prompt: Build a producer/consumer example using a thread-safe queue. Use a clear completion signal and prove that every submitted item is processed exactly once.

exercises.title: Pipe message protocol
exercises.prompt: Design a tiny pipe/message protocol where each message has a clear delimiter or length. Parse several messages correctly and handle an incomplete message without treating it as complete.

exercises.title: Socket framing simulation
exercises.prompt: Given a byte stream where one application message can arrive in multiple chunks, reconstruct complete length-prefixed messages. Demonstrate that recv/read boundaries are not message boundaries.

exercises.title: Shared-memory coordination
exercises.prompt: Model two workers accessing shared data and identify what synchronization is required to prevent one worker from observing a partially updated state. Explain the trade-off versus isolated message passing.

exercises.title: Bounded worker pool
exercises.prompt: Process a list of tasks with a fixed maximum number of concurrent workers. Record completed results and show that worker count never exceeds the configured limit.

exercises.title: Backpressure under overload
exercises.prompt: Simulate producers generating work faster than consumers. Add a bounded queue or rejection/waiting policy and demonstrate what happens when capacity is reached instead of allowing unlimited memory growth.

exercises.title: Measure before optimizing
exercises.prompt: Benchmark or profile two implementations of the same small systems task. Run multiple trials, report the measured bottleneck, and explain which change the evidence supports rather than optimizing by guesswork.

projects.title: Safe resource library
projects.description: Build Python context-manager wrappers for files, locks, and simulated system resources.

projects.title: Command pipeline runner
projects.description: Build a safe Python command-pipeline model that validates commands, captures output and exit codes, and handles failures.

projects.title: Concurrent file-processing service
projects.description: Build a bounded worker-pool service with a task queue, metrics, cancellation, and tests.

capstone.title: Concurrent systems service with observability
capstone.description: Build a Python service that accepts work, processes tasks with bounded concurrency, communicates through a clear protocol, and proves correctness with tests and metrics.

careerApplications: Used in infrastructure, performance-sensitive services, runtimes, tooling, operating-system integrations, networking, and low-level debugging roles.

quiz.q: Why use a context manager for an OS resource such as a file or lock?
options: It provides a guaranteed cleanup path even when an exception occurs
It makes the resource global forever
It prevents all I/O errors
It copies the resource into RAM

quiz.q: Resource ownership mainly answers which question?
options: Who is responsible for releasing or closing the resource and when
Which variable has the shortest name
Which CPU instruction is fastest
Which network port is public

quiz.q: Why should you not rely only on garbage collection to close critical OS resources?
options: Cleanup timing may be non-deterministic and resources can remain held too long
Garbage collection never exists in Python
It always deletes source files
It changes process exit codes

quiz.q: In Python, assignment like b = a for a mutable object usually means:
options: Both names refer to the same object unless a copy is made
A deep copy is always created
The object becomes immutable
The original object is deleted

quiz.q: Why can a shallow copy still share state?
options: Nested mutable objects can still be referenced by both copies
Shallow copies are always strings
A shallow copy disables garbage collection
It makes every nested item immutable

quiz.q: What does object identity tell you?
options: Whether two references point to the same object, not merely equal values
Whether two values print the same text only
Whether an object is stored on disk
Whether a process exited successfully

quiz.q: What is a file descriptor?
options: An operating-system handle/number referring to an open I/O resource
A Python class name for every file
A network hostname
A CPU register that stores source code

quiz.q: Why must systems code be prepared for partial reads or writes?
options: An OS call may process fewer bytes than requested, so code may need to continue until the protocol requirement is satisfied
Every OS call always handles the entire buffer
Partial I/O only occurs in databases
Python automatically retries every system call forever

quiz.q: What should you do with an OS I/O error?
options: Preserve/inspect the error information and handle or propagate it according to the operation requirements
Ignore it and claim success
Convert every error into an empty string
Retry forever with no limit

quiz.q: What does a child process exit status normally tell you?
options: Whether the program reported success or a type of failure according to its contract
How much RAM the parent owns
The current network latency
Which thread holds a lock

quiz.q: Why is passing subprocess arguments as a structured argument list often safer than building an untrusted shell command string?
options: It reduces accidental shell interpretation/injection and keeps arguments separate
It always makes the child run faster
It disables exit codes
It guarantees the command exists

quiz.q: A separate process normally has:
options: Its own virtual address space and OS-managed resources, isolated from the parent address space
Exactly the same writable memory objects as every other process
No environment or exit status
Only one possible thread

quiz.q: What is a data race?
options: A correctness problem where unsynchronized concurrent accesses depend on timing/interleaving
A benchmark between two CPUs
A file-copy operation
A deterministic queue

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a lock around shared mutable state?
options: Make a critical update mutually exclusive so conflicting operations do not interleave incorrectly
Increase network bandwidth
Create a new process
Turn a queue into a file

quiz.q: Why are thread-safe queues useful for worker communication?
options: They provide a coordinated way to hand off work/results without manually sharing every piece of mutable state
They remove all need for capacity limits
They make every task CPU-bound
They replace exception handling

quiz.q: Why does a byte-stream socket need application-level message framing?
options: One read call does not necessarily correspond to one complete application message
Sockets already preserve arbitrary Python object boundaries
Framing is only for images
It prevents all network failures

quiz.q: Which IPC mechanism naturally supports communication between processes over a network as well as locally?
options: Sockets
A normal local Python variable
A thread lock only
A function parameter after the process has started

quiz.q: Shared memory is fast but usually requires extra care with:
options: Synchronization and defining who may read/write shared regions
DNS names only
HTML parsing
Git branches

quiz.q: Why bound the size of a worker pool?
options: To control CPU/memory/I/O pressure instead of creating unlimited concurrent work
To prevent any task from finishing
To force all tasks to run serially
To remove the need for a queue

quiz.q: What is backpressure?
options: A mechanism that slows, blocks, or rejects new work when downstream capacity is full
A way to make a queue infinite
A branch-prediction technique
A file permission

quiz.q: A Future/Promise-like result represents:
options: A result that may complete later, including success or failure
A permanently locked resource
A file descriptor number only
A CPU cache line

quiz.q: What should you do before optimizing a systems bottleneck?
options: Measure/profile the workload and collect repeatable evidence
Rewrite the entire program immediately
Assume the slowest-looking function is the cause
Disable logging and tests

quiz.q: Why run a benchmark more than once?
options: To reduce the chance that startup noise or random system variation controls the conclusion
Because one run can never execute code
To make the source code longer
To guarantee identical wall-clock time

quiz.q: What can tracemalloc-style tooling help investigate?
options: Where Python memory allocations are occurring and growing
DNS routing tables
GPU shader compilation only
Git merge conflicts
